FLUIDS / SODIUM

Sodium

Identify high or low sodium → assess perfusion → recheck → plan the next interval → monitor and adjust.

1. Assess perfusion · Hypernatremia

High sodium alone is not a reason for a bolus. Hypovolemia means reduced circulating volume; dehydration is a water deficit. Address impaired perfusion while planning controlled sodium management; complete dehydration correction is not a prerequisite.

Resuscitation fluid reference · verify the bag label

LRS: Na 130 mEq/L · Plasma-Lyte / Normosol-R: Na 140 mEq/L · 0.9% NaCl: Na 154 mEq/L. Custom fluid: enter its label concentration below. These are the existing product-reference values, not a bolus prescription. Free-water replacement is a separate decision.

Recheck after initial treatment

Sodium may change during initial fluid treatment. Use the latest measurement to plan the next interval; keep earlier results to track total correction.

2. Plan the next interval

Next interval = the time until your next sodium check. Plan a small change, then adjust treatment using the measured response.

Latest recorded sodium— mEq/L

Chronic/unknown: 0.5 mEq/L/hr is a suggested upper planning rate, not a required rate or guaranteed response. Select a slower rate when appropriate. Four hours is an editable initial planning interval; monitoring may need to be sooner.

Free-water estimate · not a fluid order

ⓘ What is this for? Estimated water needed to move sodium toward the selected target. Helps plan controlled free-water replacement after addressing hypovolemia. Not a bolus volume or automatically the volume of your selected crystalloid. Account for other fluids and ongoing losses; adjust to repeat sodium measurements.

Do not automatically add this to the full dehydration deficit or shared fluid plan: estimates can overlap and need clinical reconciliation.

Total-body-water assumption & worked math

Total body water = 0.6 × body weight in kg (liters), retaining the workbook assumption. Neither this estimate nor the sodium-response equation models evolving renal handling or ongoing losses.

      Hyponatremia · measured patient sodium

      Neurologic compromise or hypoperfusion: assess and stabilize urgently. The mixing cards are not a rescue-bolus protocol.
      Hyponatremia workup & investigation

      Urgent assessment

      Seizures or marked neurologic compromise require urgent evaluation for symptomatic hyponatremia; consider other causes concurrently. Stabilize hypoperfusion with a fluid selected to avoid an abrupt sodium shift.

      AAHA describes 2–6 mL/kg of 3–7.5% NaCl over 10–15 minutes for symptomatic cases, with reassessment. The mixing cards below are not this rescue-bolus protocol.

      Confirm & investigate

      • Repeat Na if unexpected; review assay/sample issues, glucose, and other chemistry findings.
      • Review GI/renal losses, third spacing, water intake, diuretics, desmopressin, and recent fluids; assess hydration and volume status.
      • Obtain urinalysis/USG and renal assessment as indicated. Consider measured osmolality and urine studies if the cause remains unclear.
      • In dogs with compatible findings, investigate hypoadrenocorticism; consider cardiac/hepatic/renal disease or inappropriate water retention according to the examination.
      Canine Addison’s testing reference

      AAHA: resting cortisol >2 µg/dL strongly excludes hypoadrenocorticism when assay-interfering glucocorticoids are absent. A lower result is not diagnostic; confirm with ACTH stimulation when indicated. Na:K ratio alone is not diagnostic.

      Sources and limitations

      Chronic/uncertain cases: use a conservative starting plan within 0.5 mEq/L/hr and 10–12 mEq/L/day; monitor the actual response. This is a focused ER workflow, not an exhaustive differential list.

      Hyponatremia starting plan

      Uses the selected fluid card and the shared patient weight/Na. Enter all potassium in the administered fluid, including carrier K and additives; K affects this sodium-response equation.

      The per-liter Adrogué–Madias estimate is scaled to planned volume. This approximate starting estimate omits evolving losses and renal water handling; serial Na measurements take precedence.

            Existing chronic reference: ≤0.5 mEq/L/hr and 10–12 mEq/L per 24 hours. Owner-approved daily ceiling: 10 mEq/L per 24 hours (November 3, 2026). Owner-selected proposed eventual target: 158 mEq/L, editable and requiring case confirmation when no laboratory interval is configured; this is not a validated reference interval. Confirmed acute retains the existing AAHA free-water/time estimate; automatic next-interval prescribing is withheld pending an approved acute monitoring/correction protocol. Fluid reference values and the 0.6 body-water fraction retain the existing site assumptions. AAHA Tables 12C/13A were retrieved and checked November 3, 2026. Product references: LRS label · Veterinary Plasma-Lyte A label · Normosol-R label. Labels confirm LRS Na/K 130/4 and Plasma-Lyte A/Normosol-R 140/5 mEq/L. Verify the actual bag and any additives. The conservative sampled-history allowance was approved by the owner November 3, 2026; it is an application planning bound, not an AAHA formula. Software tests are not clinical validation.
